item.title: Salesforce Email Templates & Alerts Cheat Sheet: Merge Fields, Flow and Admin Interview Q&A (Day 17/30)
item.description: Write the email once, merge in the record data, and let automation send it at the right moment. Email templates and alerts are everyday admin work and a…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
Write the email once, merge in the record data, and let automation send it at the right moment. Email templates and alerts are everyday admin work and a common interview topic.

The 4 Building Blocks

Block What it is Key point
Template Reusable email layout Merge fields fill it in
Email Alert Sends a template Chosen recipients
Letterhead Logo and brand colours Wraps the template
Org-Wide Address Trusted From address Must be verified

Interview Q&A

1. What is an email template?

A reusable email with merge fields that fill in record data automatically.

Tip: Write once, reuse everywhere.

2. What template types exist?

Lightning templates use a builder. Classic ones are text, HTML and Visualforce.

Tip: Lightning is the modern default.

3. What is an email alert?

A saved action that sends a template to the recipients you choose.

Tip: The alert sends, Flow decides when.

4. How do you trigger one?

From a Flow or an approval process when your condition is met.

Tip: Use Flow for new work.

5. What are merge fields?

Placeholders like {!Contact.FirstName} swapped for real values when the email is sent.

Tip: Test with a real record.

6. What are the limits?

A daily send limit applies, and emails can bounce or land in spam.

Tip: Use an org-wide address.

Scenario Question

"Email the customer when a case is closed. How?"

  1. Create a template with merge fields

  2. Create an email alert using it

  3. Add it to a Flow on case closed

  4. Test with a real case

Quick Cheat Sheet

  • Template = reusable email

  • Alert = sends it

  • Merge field = record data

  • Letterhead = branding

  • Org-wide = trusted sender

  • Flow = decides when

Key Takeaways

  • Use merge fields, not typed names

  • Send from an org-wide address

  • Test before you activate

  • One template per purpose

Which email do you automate first? Tell me in the comments!

item.title: Salesforce Sandboxes & Change Sets Cheat Sheet: Types, Validation and Admin Interview Q&A (Day 16/30)
item.description: Build safely away from live users, then move the changes to production the controlled way. Sandboxes and change sets are core admin deployment topics and a…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
Build safely away from live users, then move the changes to production the controlled way. Sandboxes and change sets are core admin deployment topics and a favourite interview question.

The 4 Building Blocks

Block What it is Key point
Sandbox Safe copy of production Build and test here
Outbound Set Built in the source org Uploaded to the target
Inbound Set Arrives in the target org Validate, then deploy
Validation Dry run with tests Saves nothing

Interview Q&A

1. What is a sandbox?

A copy of production metadata where you build and test changes safely, away from live users.

Tip: Never build in production.

2. What are the sandbox types?

Developer and Developer Pro copy metadata. Partial Copy adds sample data. Full copies everything.

Tip: Match the type to the test.

3. What is a change set?

A bundle of metadata components you send from one org to another connected org.

Tip: Metadata only, not data.

4. Outbound vs inbound?

Outbound is built and uploaded in the source org. Inbound waits in the target org to be validated and deployed.

Tip: Outbound out, inbound in.

5. Why validate first?

A validation runs the checks and tests without saving changes, so you know the deploy will pass.

Tip: Validate, then deploy.

6. What are the limits?

Change sets work only between connected orgs, some components are unsupported, and there is no version history or easy rollback.

Tip: Name the limits, then mention Git and CI/CD.

Scenario Question

"Move a new validation rule and layout to production. How?"

  1. Build and test it in a sandbox

  2. Add both to an outbound change set

  3. Upload to production and validate

  4. Deploy in a quiet window

Quick Cheat Sheet

  • Sandbox = safe copy of prod

  • Outbound = sent from source

  • Inbound = received in target

  • Validate = dry run

  • Apex = 75% test coverage

  • Limits = no rollback

Key Takeaways

  • Build in a sandbox only

  • Add every dependency to the set

  • Validate before you deploy

  • Deploy outside business hours

What was your first deployment? Tell me in the comments!

item.title: Salesforce Data Import Wizard vs Data Loader Cheat Sheet: Upsert, Limits and Admin Interview Q&A (Day 15/30)
item.description: Two tools, one job. Pick by record volume, objects and whether you need to update or delete. This is one of the most common practical questions in a…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
Two tools, one job. Pick by record volume, objects and whether you need to update or delete. This is one of the most common practical questions in a Salesforce admin interview.

The 4 Building Blocks

Block What it is Key point
Import Wizard Browser tool for simple loads Up to 50,000 records
Data Loader Desktop app for big jobs Up to 5 million records
Upsert Update matches, insert the rest Matched by External ID
Export Back up data before a load Export or Export All

Interview Q&A

1. Wizard vs Data Loader?

The Wizard is simple and browser-based for up to 50,000 records. Data Loader handles far larger volumes and more objects.

Tip: Size and object decide.

2. What is an upsert?

It updates records that match and inserts the rest, matching on the record ID or an External ID field.

Tip: External IDs avoid duplicates.

3. What can Data Loader do?

Insert, update, upsert, delete, hard delete, export and export all, from the app or the command line.

Tip: Export All includes deleted rows.

4. How do you load related data?

Load parents first, then load children using IDs or External IDs to link them to their parents.

Tip: Parents before children.

5. What do you check after a load?

Open the success and error files, fix the failed rows, and reload only those.

Tip: Keep the error file.

6. How do you avoid a bad load?

Test in a sandbox, export a backup first, and check validation rules and automation that will fire.

Tip: Back up before you load.

Scenario Question

"Load 200,000 contacts from a CSV without duplicates. How do you do it?"

  1. Export a backup of existing contacts

  2. Clean the CSV and add an External ID

  3. Run Data Loader with upsert

  4. Check the success and error files

Quick Cheat Sheet

  • Wizard = up to 50,000 records

  • Loader = up to 5 million

  • Upsert = update or insert

  • External ID = match key

  • Parents = load first

  • Error file = fix and reload

Key Takeaways

  • Clean the data before loading

  • Test in a sandbox first

  • Export a backup beforehand

  • Keep success and error files

What was your biggest data load? Tell me in the comments!

item.title: Salesforce Permission Sets & Groups Cheat Sheet: Profiles, Muting and Admin Interview Q&A (Day 14/30)
item.description: One profile, many permission sets. Start with minimum access, then add only what each person needs. It is the access-control answer interviewers expect…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
One profile, many permission sets. Start with minimum access, then add only what each person needs. It is the access-control answer interviewers expect from a modern admin.

The 4 Building Blocks

Block What it is Key point
Permission Set Adds access on top of a profile Grants only, never removes
Set Group Bundles sets for a job role Assign one group per role
Muting Set Switches off a permission in a group Other uses stay unchanged
Assignment Many sets per user One profile per user

Interview Q&A

1. Profile vs Permission Set?

A user has one profile as the baseline, and any number of permission sets that add extra access.

Tip: One profile, many sets.

2. Why prefer permission sets?

They follow least privilege: keep profiles minimal and grant extras only to the people who need them.

Tip: Fewer profiles, easier upkeep.

3. What is a Permission Set Group?

It bundles several permission sets into one unit you assign, usually matching a job role.

Tip: Assign one group per role.

4. What is a Muting Permission Set?

It lives inside a group and turns off chosen permissions from that group's sets, without editing the sets.

Tip: Mute, do not clone.

5. Can a permission set remove access?

A normal set only grants. To take access away, use a muting set or change the profile.

Tip: Access is additive.

6. What stays on the profile?

Login hours, login IP ranges, default record types and page layout assignments still live on the profile.

Tip: Name login hours and IP ranges.

Scenario Question

"Only 10 of 100 reps may export reports. How do you do it?"

  1. Keep one shared profile for all reps

  2. Create a permission set with Export Reports

  3. Assign it to the 10 users

  4. Bundle into a group if roles grow

Quick Cheat Sheet

  • Profile = baseline, one per user

  • Set = extra access, many per user

  • Group = bundle for a role

  • Muting = off inside a group

  • Additive = sets only grant

  • Profile-only = login hours, IPs

Key Takeaways

  • Keep profiles minimal

  • Grant extra access with sets

  • Group sets by job role

  • Document what each set is for

Which access would you move to a set first? Tell me in the comments!

Following my 30-day daily blogging journey. Day 14 done, 16 to go.

item.title: Salesforce Record Types & Page Layouts Cheat Sheet: Picklists, Assignment and Admin Interview Q&A (Day 13/30)
item.description: One object, many teams. Record types and page layouts show each team the fields, values and process it needs, and they come up in almost every admin…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
One object, many teams. Record types and page layouts show each team the fields, values and process it needs, and they come up in almost every admin interview.

The 4 Building Blocks

Block What it is Key point
Record Type Splits one object into variants Own picklists and process
Page Layout Fields, buttons, related lists Assigned by profile
Picklist Values Limited per record type Hide the ones not needed
Assignment Profile plus record type Picks the layout shown

Interview Q&A

1. What is a Record Type?

It lets one object serve different teams, each with its own picklist values, page layouts and business process.

Tip: Use it when processes differ.

2. What is a Page Layout?

It controls which fields, buttons, sections and related lists a user sees on a record.

Tip: Layouts shape the screen, not security.

3. How is a layout assigned?

By profile and record type together. Each pair gets one page layout.

Tip: Check the assignment matrix.

4. How do users get a record type?

Through their profile or a permission set. Without access, they cannot pick it.

Tip: Permission sets add types without editing the profile.

5. Layout vs field-level security?

A layout only hides a field on the page. Field-level security blocks access everywhere, including reports and the API.

Tip: Use FLS to truly protect data.

6. Page Layout vs Lightning Page?

Page layouts set fields and related lists. Lightning record pages set the overall page, components and dynamic forms.

Tip: Name both, then say which you use.

Scenario Question

"Support handles Billing and Technical cases with different fields. How do you do it?"

  1. Create two Case record types

  2. Limit the Status values for each type

  3. Build one page layout for each type

  4. Assign by profile and record type

Quick Cheat Sheet

  • Record type = variant of an object

  • Layout = fields and related lists

  • Picklist = values per type

  • Access = profile or permission set

  • FLS = real field security

  • Lightning page = overall page

Key Takeaways

  • Add types only when processes differ

  • Keep layouts simple and few

  • Never rely on layouts for security

  • Test as a real user

Which object would you split first? Tell me in the comments!

item.title: Salesforce Approval Processes Cheat Sheet: Entry Criteria, Approvers and Admin Interview Q&A (Day 12/30)
item.description: Some changes need a second pair of eyes. Approval processes route a record to the right person before it moves on, and they come up in almost every admin…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
Some changes need a second pair of eyes. Approval processes route a record to the right person before it moves on, and they come up in almost every admin interview that touches automation.

The 4 Building Blocks

Block What it is Key point
Entry Criteria Decides which records can be submitted Records that miss them cannot be submitted
Approval Step Who reviews the record User, queue, manager or field
Actions Run on submit, approve or reject Field update, email, task
Record Lock Record is read-only while pending Admins can still edit

Interview Q&A

1. What is an Approval Process?

It automates how a record gets approved: submit, route to approvers, then approve or reject, with actions at each stage.

Tip: Think of it as a manager sign-off.

2. What are entry criteria?

Conditions a record must meet before it can be submitted, like Discount over 20 percent.

Tip: Records that miss them cannot be submitted.

3. Who can be an approver?

A user, a queue, the submitter's manager, or a user picked from a field on the record.

Tip: Queues let a team share the work.

4. What actions can run?

Field updates, email alerts, tasks and outbound messages, on submit, final approval, final rejection or recall.

Tip: Use a field update to set Status.

5. What does the record lock do?

A pending record is locked so users cannot edit it. Admins can still edit, and a recall unlocks it.

Tip: The lock stops edits while review is open.

6. Approval Process vs Flow?

Approval Processes handle classic sign-off. Flow Orchestrator is the newer option for complex, multi-step approvals.

Tip: Name the trade-off, then pick.

Scenario Question

"Discounts over 20 percent need manager approval before the deal moves on. How do you do it?"

  1. Entry criteria: Discount greater than 20 percent

  2. Approver: the submitter's manager

  3. On submit: a field update sets Status to Pending

  4. On approval: Status becomes Approved

Quick Cheat Sheet

  • Entry = who may submit

  • Approver = user, queue, manager

  • Actions = update, email, task

  • Lock = read-only while pending

  • Recall = pulls it back

  • Orchestrator = newer option

Key Takeaways

  • Define entry criteria first

  • Prefer queues or managers over named users

  • Track status with field updates

  • Test with a real submitter

What would you send for approval first? Tell me in the comments!

Following my 30-day daily blogging journey. Day 12 done, 18 to go.

item.title: Salesforce Validation Rules Cheat Sheet: Formulas, Error Messages and Admin Interview Q&A (Day 11/30)
item.description: Clean data starts at the door. Validation rules decide what Salesforce lets in, and what it turns away. They are one of the most asked-about admin topics…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
Clean data starts at the door. Validation rules decide what Salesforce lets in, and what it turns away. They are one of the most asked-about admin topics because every real org depends on them.

The 4 Data Quality Tools

Tool What it is Key point
Validation Rule Blocks a save if the formula is TRUE Shows your error message
Formula Field A read-only calculated value Recalculates automatically
Required Field Must have a value to save Set on the field or the layout
Duplicate Rule Warns or blocks likely duplicates Works with Matching Rules

Interview Q&A

1. What is a Validation Rule?

A formula that returns TRUE when data is bad. If it is TRUE, Salesforce blocks the save and shows your error message.

Tip: TRUE means error, FALSE means save.

2. Where does the error show?

You choose: at the top of the page, or next to a specific field on the record page.

Tip: Show it by the field the user must fix.

3. Required field vs Validation Rule?

A field-level required setting always applies, even through the API. A validation rule can add conditions, like required only at a certain stage.

Tip: Needed only sometimes? Use a rule.

4. Formula field vs Validation Rule?

A formula field returns a value users cannot edit. A validation rule formula returns TRUE or FALSE to allow or block a save.

Tip: Formula fields are read-only.

5. Which functions come up most?

ISBLANK for empty checks, ISPICKVAL for picklists, AND and OR to combine tests, ISCHANGED on updates, and REGEX for patterns.

Tip: Never compare a picklist with =.

6. Do rules run on imports and Flows?

Yes. They also run for the API, Apex and Flow. To skip them for admins or data loads, check a custom permission in the formula.

Tip: Avoid hardcoding profile names.

Scenario Question

"Reps must not mark an Opportunity Closed Won without an Amount. How do you enforce it?"

  1. Go to Object Manager, Opportunity, Validation Rules

  2. Write the formula with ISPICKVAL and ISBLANK

  3. Add a clear error message on the Amount field

  4. Test in a sandbox, then activate

The formula looks like this:

AND(
  ISPICKVAL(StageName, "Closed Won"),
  ISBLANK(Amount)
)

Quick Cheat Sheet

  • TRUE = block the save

  • ISBLANK = empty check

  • ISPICKVAL = picklist check

  • ISCHANGED = on updates

  • Formula field = read-only

  • Bypass = custom permission

Key Takeaways

  • Write the rule so TRUE means bad data

  • Keep error messages specific

  • Required field for always, rule for sometimes

  • Add a bypass for data loads

What is the best validation rule you have written? Tell me in the comments!

Following my 30-day daily blogging journey. Day 11 done, 19 to go.

item.title: Salesforce Reports & Dashboards Cheat Sheet: Formats, Running User and Admin Interview Q&A (Day 10/30)
item.description: Reports answer the question, dashboards show the answer. Interviewers love this topic because it tests whether you can turn raw data into something a…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
Reports answer the question, dashboards show the answer. Interviewers love this topic because it tests whether you can turn raw data into something a manager can act on.

The 4 Report Formats

Format What it is Key point
Tabular A simple list of records No grouping, no dashboard charts
Summary Rows grouped by a field Up to 3 groupings, subtotals
Matrix Grouped by rows and columns Up to 2 row and 2 column groups
Joined Blocks from different report types Up to 5 blocks in one report

Interview Q&A

1. What is a Report Type?

It decides which objects and fields a report can use. Standard report types exist, and you can build custom report types with related objects.

Tip: "With" shows parents that have children, "with or without" shows all parents.

2. Summary vs Matrix report?

A Summary report groups rows by up to 3 fields. A Matrix report groups by both rows and columns, so you can compare two dimensions at once.

Tip: Need a cross-tab like region by quarter? Use a matrix.

3. Report vs Dashboard?

A report lists filtered records. A dashboard shows up to 20 components, each built from a source report.

Tip: Every component needs a source report.

4. Running user vs dynamic dashboard?

A normal dashboard shows data as seen by its running user. A dynamic dashboard runs as whoever is viewing it.

Tip: Use dynamic when each viewer should see only their own data.

5. What is a Bucket field?

It groups report values into categories you define, with no formula or custom field needed.

Tip: For example, group deal amounts into Small, Medium and Large.

6. What is a Cross filter?

It filters records by related records, like Accounts with or without Opportunities.

Tip: Great for finding accounts with no activity.

Scenario Question

"A sales manager wants open pipeline by stage as a dashboard, emailed weekly. How do you do it?"

  1. Build a Summary report on Opportunities, open only

  2. Group the report by Stage and add a chart

  3. Add it to a dashboard as a component

  4. Subscribe the manager for a weekly email

Quick Cheat Sheet

  • Tabular = simple list

  • Summary = up to 3 groupings

  • Matrix = rows and columns

  • Joined = up to 5 blocks

  • Dashboard = up to 20 components

  • Bucket = group without a formula

Key Takeaways

  • Choose the report type first

  • Summary to group, matrix to compare

  • Dashboards display reports

  • Check the running user

Summary or Matrix: which do you build most? Tell me in the comments!

Following my 30-day daily blogging journey. Day 10 done, 20 to go.

item.title: Lookup vs Master-Detail: Salesforce Relationships Cheat Sheet for Admin Interviews (Day 9/30)
item.description: Relationships are the backbone of every Salesforce data model, and interviewers love them. Almost every question comes down to one idea: can the child…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
Relationships are the backbone of every Salesforce data model, and interviewers love them. Almost every question comes down to one idea: can the child record exist without its parent?

The 4 Relationship Types

Type What it is Key point
Lookup A loose link between two objects Optional, the child keeps its own owner
Master-Detail A tight parent-child bond Cascade delete, roll-ups, shared access
Junction object Links two objects many-to-many Two master-detail fields
Hierarchical Records link to the same object Parent Account, user manager

Interview Q&A

1. Standard vs Custom objects?

Standard objects ship with Salesforce, such as Account, Contact and Opportunity. Custom objects are built by you, and their API names end in __c.

Tip: Custom objects and fields always end in __c.

2. Lookup vs Master-Detail?

A Lookup is optional and loosely coupled. A Master-Detail is required: the child inherits the parent's owner and sharing.

Tip: Ask: can the child exist without the parent?

3. What is a Junction object?

A custom object with two master-detail fields that creates a many-to-many link, like Student to Course through Enrollment.

Tip: The first master-detail sets the owner and sharing.

4. What is a Roll-up Summary field?

It lives on the master record and calculates COUNT, SUM, MIN or MAX over its detail records. It is only available with master-detail.

Tip: Need it on a lookup? Use a Flow instead.

5. Can you convert between them?

Lookup to Master-Detail works only if every child record already has a parent. Master-Detail to Lookup works only if the parent has no roll-up summary fields.

Tip: Fill in blank lookups before converting.

6. What happens if the parent is deleted?

With Master-Detail the children are deleted too (cascade). With a Lookup the children stay, unless you restrict the delete.

Tip: Restricting delete protects child data.

Scenario Question

"A school tracks Students and Courses, and each student can take many courses. How do you model it?"

  1. Create custom objects Student and Course

  2. Create a junction object called Enrollment

  3. Add two master-detail fields: one to Student, one to Course

  4. Add a roll-up summary on Course to count Enrollments

Quick Cheat Sheet

  • Lookup = optional, independent

  • Master-Detail = required, cascade delete

  • Junction = two master-details

  • Roll-up = master-detail only

  • Max 2 master-detail fields per object

  • Custom API names end in __c

Key Takeaways

  • Start with: can the child exist alone?

  • Use master-detail for tight ownership

  • Use a junction object for many-to-many

  • Plan relationships before you build

Lookup or Master-Detail: which do you pick first? Tell me in the comments!

Following my 30-day daily blogging journey. Day 9 done, 21 to go.

item.title: Salesforce Flow Cheat Sheet: Types, Triggers and Admin Interview Q&A (Day 8/30)
item.description: Flow is now the one automation tool every Salesforce Admin is expected to know. Interviewers usually ask the same few things: which type, which trigger…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
Flow is now the one automation tool every Salesforce Admin is expected to know. Interviewers usually ask the same few things: which type, which trigger timing, and how you keep it safe at scale.

The 4 Flow Types

Type Use it when Examples
Screen Flow A user needs to click and type Guided forms, wizards, Lightning pages
Record-Triggered Flow A record is created, updated or deleted Update a field, create a task
Scheduled-Triggered Flow Something must run at a set time Daily or weekly batch jobs
Autolaunched Flow Another process calls it Called from flows, Apex, buttons

Interview Q&A

1. What is a Record-Triggered Flow?

It runs automatically when a record is created, updated or deleted. Entry conditions decide when it actually fires.

Tip: Add entry conditions so it only runs when needed.

2. Before-save vs After-save?

Before-save updates the same record that triggered the flow, fast, with no extra DML. After-save handles related records, emails and other actions.

Tip: Same record = before. Anything else = after.

3. Flow vs Workflow Rules and Process Builder?

Workflow Rules and Process Builder are retired, with support ending on Dec 31, 2025. Flow is the single automation tool going forward.

Tip: Say you would migrate old automation to Flow.

4. Flow or Apex?

Start with clicks, not code. Use Apex when logic is very complex, needs heavy bulk processing, or Flow cannot do it.

Tip: "Declarative first" is the safe answer.

5. What are the data elements?

Get, Create, Update and Delete Records. Get Records reads data into variables you can reuse.

Tip: One well-filtered Get Records beats many.

6. Why never put DML in a loop?

Governor limits cap queries and DML per transaction. Collect records in a collection variable, then do one DML after the loop.

Tip: Add a Fault path and test with Debug.

Scenario Question

"When an Opportunity becomes Closed Won, create a follow-up Task and update the Account. How?"

  1. Build a Record-Triggered Flow on Opportunity, run after save

  2. Entry condition: Stage = Closed Won and Stage is changed

  3. Create Records: a Task for the Account owner

  4. Update Records: the Account, add a Fault path, then test with Debug

Quick Cheat Sheet

  • Screen = user input

  • Record-Triggered = on create, update, delete

  • Scheduled = runs at a set time

  • Autolaunched = called by others

  • Before-save = fast, same record

  • No DML in loops

Key Takeaways

  • Flow first, Apex only when needed

  • Choose before-save or after-save on purpose

  • Use entry conditions to limit runs

  • Always add Fault paths and test with Debug

Which Flow type do you use most? Tell me in the comments!

Following my 30-day daily blogging journey. Day 8 done, 22 to go.

item.title: Salesforce Security Model Cheat Sheet: 4 Layers and Admin Interview Q&A (Day 7/30)
item.description: Security questions come up in almost every Salesforce Admin interview. The good news: the whole model fits in one picture. Think of it as four locks on…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
Security questions come up in almost every Salesforce Admin interview. The good news: the whole model fits in one picture. Think of it as four locks on four doors, and every question is really asking "which lock is this?"

This is the quick cheat sheet version. For the long, step-by-step walkthrough, read my earlier post: The Salesforce Security Model Explained: OWD, Roles, Sharing Rules and More.

The Big Picture: 4 Layers of Access

Layer Question it answers Tools
Org level Can this person log in at all? Password policies, login hours, login IP ranges, MFA
Object level Can they see or edit this type of data? Profiles, Permission Sets
Field level Can they see this column? Field-Level Security (FLS)
Record level Can they see this row? OWD, Role Hierarchy, Sharing Rules, Manual Sharing

Golden rule: Object and field access decide what kind of data you can touch. Record access decides which rows you can touch. You need both.

Interview Q&A

1. What is a Profile?

A profile controls what a user can do: which objects and fields they can access, which apps and tabs they see, and system permissions. Every user has exactly one profile.

Tip: Say "profile = baseline permissions". It sets up your next answer about permission sets.

2. What is a Permission Set, and how is it different from a Profile?

A permission set adds access on top of a profile. A user can have many permission sets, but only one profile. Permission sets can only grant access, never take it away.

Tip: Mention best practice: keep profiles minimal and grant extra access through permission sets (and Permission Set Groups to bundle them).

3. What is OWD (Organization-Wide Defaults)?

OWD sets the baseline record access for each object. It is the most restrictive level in the system, and every other tool (roles, sharing rules) can only open access up from there.

Common settings: Private, Public Read Only, Public Read/Write, Controlled by Parent.

Tip: Always say "start restrictive, then open up".

4. What is the Role Hierarchy?

Roles control record visibility upward. A manager can see the records owned by people below them in the hierarchy. Roles do not give object permissions; that is the profile's job.

Tip: The classic trap question: "Profile vs Role?" Profile = what you can do. Role = which records you can see.

5. What are Sharing Rules?

Sharing rules open access to records for groups of users when OWD is restrictive. They can be based on record owner or on record criteria (for example, Region = West).

Tip: Remember sharing rules only extend access. They can never restrict it.

6. What is Field-Level Security?

FLS controls whether a user can see or edit a specific field, set through profiles or permission sets. Hidden fields disappear from page layouts, reports and list views.

Tip: A page layout alone does not secure a field. FLS does.

7. What is Manual Sharing?

The record owner (or a user with full access) can share an individual record with a specific user or group. It is useful for one-off exceptions.

Tip: Manual sharing is lost if the record owner changes, so don't build a process around it.

8. If two settings conflict, which one wins?

Access in Salesforce is additive: the most permissive result wins. Two permission sources never cancel each other out.

Scenario Question (Very Common!)

"Sales reps should only see their own accounts. Managers should see their team's accounts. How do you set that up?"

  1. Set Account OWD = Private

  2. Build the Role Hierarchy with managers above reps

  3. Keep Grant Access Using Hierarchies enabled

  4. If one team needs to see another team's accounts, add a Sharing Rule

Result: reps see their own records, managers see their whole team's, no extra code needed.

Quick Cheat Sheet

  • Profile = baseline permissions (one per user)

  • Permission Set = extra permissions (many per user)

  • OWD = the most restrictive baseline for records

  • Role Hierarchy = upward record visibility

  • Sharing Rules = open access to groups

  • FLS = field-level visibility

  • Most permissive wins

Key Takeaways

  • Answer in layers: org, object, field, record

  • Use a real example for every answer

  • Always separate "what you can do" (profile) from "what you can see" (role)

  • Keep it simple, and explain why each tool exists

Which part of the Salesforce security model confused you the most when you were learning it? Tell me in the comments!

Following my 30-day daily blogging journey. Day 7 done, 23 to go.

item.title: AWS VPC for Beginners: Subnets, Route Tables, Gateways and Security Groups
item.description: Beginner's guide to AWS VPC: CIDR blocks, public and private subnets, internet and NAT gateways, route tables, security groups and NACLs.
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
A Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) is your own private network inside AWS. Every EC2 instance, RDS database and many Lambda functions live in one. Networking was the part of AWS that confused me most at first, so here is the explanation I wish I'd had.

The VPC and its CIDR block

When you create a VPC, you give it an IP range in CIDR notation, for example:

10.0.0.0/16   →   65,536 addresses (10.0.0.0 – 10.0.255.255)

A VPC lives in one region but spans all of that region's Availability Zones.

Subnets

A subnet is a slice of the VPC's range in one Availability Zone:

10.0.1.0/24   public subnet   (AZ a)
10.0.2.0/24   public subnet   (AZ b)
10.0.11.0/24  private subnet  (AZ a)
10.0.12.0/24  private subnet  (AZ b)

AWS reserves 5 addresses in every subnet, so a /24 gives you 251 usable IPs.

Public vs private isn't a setting. It depends on the subnet's route table.

Internet Gateway

An Internet Gateway (IGW) connects the VPC to the internet. A subnet is public when its route table sends internet traffic to the IGW:

Destination     Target
10.0.0.0/16     local
0.0.0.0/0       igw-xxxx

Instances in it also need a public IP to be reachable.

NAT Gateway

Instances in private subnets often still need to reach the internet (to download updates, for example) without being reachable from it. A NAT Gateway sits in a public subnet and handles that:

Private subnet route table
Destination     Target
10.0.0.0/16     local
0.0.0.0/0       nat-xxxx

NAT Gateways are charged per hour plus per GB processed, so they're often one of the bigger networking costs. For high availability, use one per AZ.

Route tables

Every subnet is associated with one route table. The local route (VPC CIDR → local) is always there, so everything inside the VPC can talk to everything else unless security rules block it.

Security groups vs network ACLs

Security Group Network ACL
Applies to Network interfaces (instances) Subnets
Rules Allow only Allow and deny
State Stateful (return traffic allowed automatically) Stateless (must allow return traffic explicitly)
Evaluation All rules together In number order, first match wins

In practice, security groups do most of the work. A common pattern is referencing one security group from another, for example: "the database security group allows port 5432 only from the app security group."

A classic three-tier layout

Internet
   │
Internet Gateway
   │
Public subnets   →  Load balancer, NAT Gateway
   │
Private subnets  →  App servers (EC2 / ECS)
   │
Private subnets  →  Database (RDS)

Only the load balancer is exposed. App servers and databases stay private.

Other pieces you'll meet

  • VPC endpoints – reach services like S3 or DynamoDB privately, without a NAT Gateway (and often more cheaply)
  • VPC peering / Transit Gateway – connect VPCs together
  • VPC Flow Logs – record traffic metadata for troubleshooting and security

Troubleshooting connectivity

When something can't connect, check in this order:

  1. Route table of the source subnet
  2. Security group on the destination (inbound) and source (outbound)
  3. Network ACLs on both subnets (remember return traffic)
  4. Public IP / Elastic IP if internet access is involved
  5. VPC Flow Logs to see whether traffic was accepted or rejected

Once you can draw your VPC on paper, most networking problems become much easier to solve.

item.title: Salesforce Sandbox Types Explained: Developer, Developer Pro, Partial Copy and Full
item.description: The four Salesforce sandbox types compared: storage, data, refresh intervals and which one to use for development, testing, UAT and training.
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
A sandbox is a copy of your production org used for building and testing without touching real users. Salesforce offers four types, and picking the right one for each stage of your release process saves a lot of pain.

The four types at a glance

Type Copies metadata Copies data Storage (data / files) Refresh interval
Developer Yes No 200 MB / 200 MB 1 day
Developer Pro Yes No 1 GB / 1 GB 1 day
Partial Copy Yes Sample (via template) 5 GB / same as prod 5 days
Full Yes All (or selected objects) Same as production 29 days

All sandboxes copy your metadata (objects, fields, flows, Apex, layouts and so on). The difference is how much data comes with it and how often you can refresh. Which types and how many you get depends on your edition and any add-ons.

Developer sandbox

Small and quick to refresh. Ideal for:

  • An individual admin or developer building a feature
  • Trying out a new flow or configuration
  • Learning and experimenting

You create the test data you need yourself.

Developer Pro sandbox

The same idea with more storage. Useful when:

  • You need larger test data sets
  • You're doing integration development
  • Several people share the environment

Partial Copy sandbox

Includes a sample of production data chosen by a sandbox template (you pick objects; Salesforce copies up to 10,000 records per object). Good for:

  • QA and integration testing with realistic data
  • Testing reports, sharing and automation against real-looking records

Full sandbox

A complete replica of production, including all data (or the objects you select). Use it for:

  • User acceptance testing (UAT)
  • Performance and load testing
  • Staging: the final check before a production release
  • Training on real-world data

The 29-day refresh interval means you need to plan when you refresh it.

A typical setup

Developer sandboxes  →  Developer Pro / Partial (QA)  →  Full (UAT/Staging)  →  Production

Each person builds in their own Developer sandbox, changes are combined and tested in QA, business users sign off in UAT, and then you deploy to production.

Tips

  • Mask sensitive data. Production data in sandboxes is still personal data. Use Data Mask or scripts to anonymise it.
  • Check email deliverability. New sandboxes default to "System email only" so you don't email real customers. Keep it that way unless you need to test emails.
  • Re-run post-refresh steps. Use a SandboxPostCopy Apex class to automate tasks such as updating integration endpoints and creating test users.
  • Mind the user emails. Sandbox users' emails get .invalid appended so they can't receive mail by accident. Fix only the ones you need.
  • Know the difference from scratch orgs. Scratch orgs are short-lived, source-driven orgs created from a definition file, which suits CI pipelines. Sandboxes are copies of production, which suits integration testing and UAT.

Choosing the right sandbox for each stage keeps development fast and testing realistic, without risking production.

item.title: Dockerfile Best Practices: Smaller, Faster and Safer Images
item.description: Practical Dockerfile best practices: multi-stage builds, layer caching, small base images, non-root users and .dockerignore, with examples.
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
Writing a Dockerfile that works is easy. Writing one that builds fast, produces a small image and doesn't run as root takes a few habits. Here are the ones that made the biggest difference for me.

1. Start from a small, specific base image

# Avoid
FROM node:latest

# Prefer
FROM node:20-alpine
  • Pin a version. latest changes under you and makes builds unreproducible.
  • Use slim or alpine variants when your app supports them. Smaller images pull faster and have fewer packages to patch.
  • For compiled languages, consider distroless or scratch for the final image.

2. Order instructions for layer caching

Docker caches each layer. If a layer changes, every layer after it is rebuilt. Put things that change rarely first:

WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
COPY . .

Now changing your source code doesn't re-run npm ci. Dependencies are only reinstalled when package.json changes.

3. Use multi-stage builds

Build tools don't belong in production images. A multi-stage build compiles in one stage and copies only the output into a clean final stage:

# Build stage
FROM node:20-alpine AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

# Runtime stage
FROM node:20-alpine
WORKDIR /app
ENV NODE_ENV=production
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist
USER node
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]

The final image contains no dev dependencies, compilers or source files it doesn't need.

4. Add a .dockerignore

Without it, COPY . . sends everything to the build context, including node_modules, .git and possibly secrets.

node_modules
.git
.env
*.log
dist

This speeds up builds and keeps sensitive files out of the image.

5. Don't run as root

Containers run as root by default. If an attacker breaks out of your app, root makes it worse. Many official images include a non-root user (node in Node images). Otherwise create one:

RUN addgroup -S app && adduser -S app -G app
USER app

6. Combine and clean up RUN steps

Each RUN creates a layer. Clean up in the same layer you create files in, or the files still take space:

RUN apt-get update \
    && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends curl \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

7. Never bake secrets into images

Anything in an image layer can be extracted, even if a later layer deletes it. Pass secrets at runtime (environment variables from a secrets manager, mounted files) or use BuildKit's --mount=type=secret for build-time secrets.

8. Prefer exec-form CMD and ENTRYPOINT

CMD ["node", "server.js"]   # exec form: receives signals properly
CMD node server.js          # shell form: wraps in /bin/sh

The exec form lets your process receive SIGTERM directly, so containers stop cleanly.

9. Add a HEALTHCHECK (when not using an orchestrator's probes)

HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s \
  CMD wget -qO- http://localhost:3000/health || exit 1

On Kubernetes you'd use liveness and readiness probes instead.

10. Scan your images

Tools like Trivy, Docker Scout or Snyk find known vulnerabilities in base images and dependencies. Run them in CI so problems are caught before deployment.

Quick checklist

  • Pinned, minimal base image
  • Dependencies copied and installed before source code
  • Multi-stage build
  • .dockerignore in place
  • Non-root USER
  • No secrets in layers
  • Image scanned in CI

Small changes, but together they often cut image size by more than half and make builds noticeably faster.

item.title: The Salesforce Security Model Explained: OWD, Roles, Sharing Rules and More
item.description: A clear walkthrough of Salesforce's layered security model: org, object, field and record-level access, with OWD, role hierarchy and sharing rules.
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
"Why can't this user see that record?" is one of the most common questions a Salesforce admin gets. The answer is almost always somewhere in the security model, which works in layers. Once you know the layers, troubleshooting becomes a checklist.

Layer 1: Org-level access

Who can log in at all, and when.

  • Active user and license
  • Login hours and login IP ranges (on profiles)
  • Multi-factor authentication
  • Session settings

Layer 2: Object-level access

Can the user work with this type of record at all? Controlled by profiles and permission sets with Create, Read, Edit, Delete, View All and Modify All.

If a user has no Read on Opportunity, nothing else matters. They won't see any opportunities.

Layer 3: Field-level security

Within an object, which fields can the user see or edit? Also set on profiles and permission sets.

Removing a field from a page layout only hides it from that layout. It does not secure it. The field can still appear in reports, list views and the API. Use field-level security for real restrictions.

Layer 4: Record-level access (sharing)

Which individual records can the user see? This is where most of the complexity lives.

Organization-Wide Defaults (OWD)

OWD sets the baseline for each object:

  • Private – only the owner (and people above them in the role hierarchy) can see it
  • Public Read Only – everyone can see, only the owner can edit
  • Public Read/Write – everyone can see and edit
  • Controlled by Parent – for detail records in a master-detail relationship

Rule of thumb: set OWD to the most restrictive level anyone needs, then open access up. Sharing can only grant access, never take it away.

Role hierarchy

Users higher in the hierarchy can see records owned by users below them (for standard objects this is always on; for custom objects it is controlled by the "Grant Access Using Hierarchies" setting). Roles reflect data visibility, not necessarily the org chart.

Sharing rules

Sharing rules open access to groups of users:

  • Owner-based – share records owned by the Sales India role with the Support India role
  • Criteria-based – share all Cases where Region = APAC with a public group

Teams and manual sharing

  • Account, Opportunity and Case Teams give specific people access to specific records.
  • Manual sharing lets an owner share one record with someone.

Restriction rules

Restriction rules go the other way: they limit which records a user can see even when they would otherwise have access. They're useful for cases like letting users see only the records relevant to their region.

A troubleshooting checklist

When a user can't see or edit something:

  1. Is the user active with the right license?
  2. Does their profile or a permission set grant object access?
  3. Is field-level security hiding the field?
  4. What is the OWD for the object?
  5. Where are they in the role hierarchy relative to the owner?
  6. Does a sharing rule, team or manual share apply?
  7. Is a restriction rule limiting them?

Use Sharing Settings, the record's Sharing Hierarchy button and the "View Summary" on a user's permissions to check quickly.

Profiles vs permission sets

Salesforce is moving towards permission sets and permission set groups as the main way to grant access, with profiles kept minimal. I'll cover that in a dedicated post later this month.

Get the layers straight and most "I can't see it" tickets take minutes instead of hours.

item.title: AWS IAM Explained: Users, Groups, Roles and Policies for Beginners
item.description: A beginner-friendly guide to AWS IAM: users, groups, roles, policies, least privilege and the mistakes to avoid.
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
Almost every AWS problem I've debugged as a beginner came back to one thing: permissions. AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) decides who can do what in your account, so it's worth understanding properly before anything else.

The four building blocks

Users

An IAM user is an identity for a person or an application that needs long-term credentials (a password for the console, or access keys for the CLI).

Best practice today is to avoid long-lived access keys where you can. For people, use IAM Identity Center (single sign-on). For workloads, use roles.

Groups

A group is a collection of users. You attach permissions to the group, and every user in it inherits them. For example, a Developers group might get read access to CloudWatch logs and permission to deploy Lambda functions.

Groups cannot contain other groups, and a group is not an identity you can log in as.

Roles

A role is an identity with permissions but no permanent credentials. Something assumes the role and gets temporary credentials. Roles are used by:

  • EC2 instances (via an instance profile)
  • Lambda functions (the execution role)
  • Other AWS accounts (cross-account access)
  • CI/CD systems such as GitHub Actions (via OpenID Connect)
  • People signing in through SSO

If you remember one thing from this post: prefer roles over access keys.

Policies

A policy is a JSON document that allows or denies actions. Here's a small example that allows reading objects from one S3 bucket:

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": ["s3:GetObject"],
      "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::my-app-bucket/*"
    }
  ]
}

Every statement has an Effect (Allow or Deny), Actions, Resources and optionally Conditions.

How AWS evaluates permissions

  1. By default, everything is denied.
  2. An explicit Allow in a policy grants access.
  3. An explicit Deny anywhere always wins over an Allow.

Other layers can also restrict access, such as Service Control Policies in AWS Organizations, permission boundaries and resource-based policies (like S3 bucket policies).

Policy types you'll meet

  • AWS managed policies – prebuilt by AWS (for example ReadOnlyAccess). Convenient but often broader than you need.
  • Customer managed policies – written by you and reusable across users, groups and roles.
  • Inline policies – embedded directly in one identity. Use them sparingly.

Least privilege in practice

"Least privilege" means granting only what's needed. Practical ways to get there:

  • Start from a managed policy, then narrow it down to specific actions and resources.
  • Use IAM Access Analyzer to generate policies from real CloudTrail activity and to find resources shared outside your account.
  • Check the Last accessed information on users and roles to remove unused permissions.

Common beginner mistakes

  • Using the root user for daily work. Lock it down with MFA and use it only for the few tasks that require it.
  • Committing access keys to Git. Use roles, or store secrets in a secrets manager.
  • "Action": "*" and "Resource": "*" everywhere. It works, until it becomes a security incident.
  • Not enabling MFA for human users.

Quick checklist

  • MFA on the root user, root access keys deleted
  • People sign in through IAM Identity Center or users with MFA
  • Applications use roles, not access keys
  • Permissions granted to groups and roles, not individual users
  • Access Analyzer enabled

IAM looks dry, but once it clicks, the rest of AWS becomes much easier to reason about. Tomorrow I'll switch to Salesforce and look at its security model.

item.title: From Operations to Salesforce and DevOps: How I Switched Careers
item.description: How I moved from 4+ years in operations roles into Salesforce administration and AWS DevOps, and what I'd tell anyone making the same switch.
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
For more than four years I worked in operations and process-driven roles. The work taught me a lot about SLAs, escalations, documentation and keeping things running when volumes spike. In July 2022 I decided to move into Salesforce administration and AWS Cloud/DevOps, and I've been building towards it ever since.

This post is about how I approached the switch, what worked, and what I'd do differently.

Why Salesforce and DevOps?

Both fields reward the same habits operations work builds:

  • Process thinking. Salesforce admins design approval processes, flows and data rules. DevOps engineers design pipelines. Both are about turning a messy manual process into a repeatable one.
  • Attention to detail. A wrong sharing rule or a missing IAM permission causes the same kind of incident a missed step in an ops runbook does.
  • Working with users. Admins and support engineers spend a lot of time understanding what people actually need, which is something operations teaches every day.

The two areas also connect. Salesforce DevOps (source control, CI/CD for metadata, tools like Copado and GitHub Actions) sits right between them.

How I learned

1. Certifications as a structured syllabus

I used certifications as a roadmap rather than a goal in themselves. So far I've earned 11, including:

  • AWS Certified DevOps Engineer – Professional
  • AWS Certified AI Practitioner and Cloud Practitioner
  • Salesforce Platform Administrator I and II, Platform App Builder, Agentforce Specialist
  • GitHub Foundations, GitHub Actions and Copado AI

Each exam forced me to cover topics I would have skipped on my own.

2. Trailhead every day

Trailhead's hands-on challenges check your work in a real org, which is the closest thing to on-the-job practice when you're starting out. I'm now a Double Star Ranger with 250+ badges and 7 superbadges. Superbadges in particular are worth the effort because they read like small real projects.

3. Building projects, not just watching videos

Tutorials feel productive, but you only find the gaps when you build something yourself. My most useful project so far is a Salesforce CI/CD pipeline that validates every pull request in a scratch org with GitHub Actions.

4. Writing it down

This blog exists because explaining something is the fastest way to find out whether you understand it.

What I'd tell someone starting today

  1. Pick one track first. Salesforce admin or AWS. Trying to learn everything at once slows you down.
  2. Get one certification early. It gives you vocabulary and confidence.
  3. Build in public. A GitHub repo and a blog post about it are worth more than a list of courses.
  4. Use your past experience. Operations, support, finance and sales backgrounds are an advantage for admin and support roles, not a gap to hide.
  5. Be consistent. An hour a day beats a weekend binge once a month.

What's next

Over the next month I'll publish a post every morning on Salesforce administration, AWS and DevOps: the practical topics I wish I'd had clear explanations for when I started.

If you're making a similar switch, I'd love to hear how it's going. Connect with me on LinkedIn.

item.title: Building a Salesforce CI/CD Pipeline with GitHub Actions and Scratch Orgs
item.description: How I built a Salesforce metadata CI/CD pipeline with GitHub Actions and scratch orgs that deploys and runs Apex tests on every pull request.
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
Most Salesforce teams still move changes between orgs by hand: build in a sandbox, add components to a change set, upload, validate, deploy, and hope nothing was missed. I wanted to see what the "real" DevOps way looks like on the Salesforce platform, so I built a small metadata CI/CD pipeline from scratch using Salesforce DX, GitHub Actions and scratch orgs.

In this post I'll walk through what the pipeline does, how it's wired together, and the one problem that cost me the most time.

Repo: github.com/RobinSishodia/salesforce-devops-pipeline

The goal

Every pull request into main should be checked automatically before anyone merges it:

  1. Spin up a brand-new, empty scratch org
  2. Deploy all the metadata from the branch into it
  3. Run the Apex tests with code coverage
  4. Delete the scratch org, pass or fail

If the deploy or any test fails, the PR shows a red check and the change doesn't go in. This is the same "validate before merge" idea used in any CI pipeline, applied to Salesforce metadata.

What you need

  • A Salesforce Developer Edition org with Dev Hub enabled (Setup → Dev Hub). The Dev Hub is the org that is allowed to create scratch orgs.
  • The Salesforce CLI (sf), VS Code and Git
  • A GitHub repository for the Salesforce DX project
  • A connected app in the Dev Hub configured for JWT (certificate-based) login, so GitHub Actions can log in without a browser

Project structure

The repo is a standard Salesforce DX project:

force-app/main/default/            # metadata source (Apex, objects, LWC...)
config/project-scratch-def.json    # what the scratch org should look like
sfdx-project.json                  # project manifest
.github/workflows/validate-pr.yml  # the pipeline

Working "source-first" like this is the key shift: the Git repo, not an org, is the source of truth.

Step 1: Let GitHub Actions log in to the Dev Hub

CI can't click through a browser login, so I used the JWT bearer flow:

  1. Generate a private key and self-signed certificate with OpenSSL
  2. Upload the certificate to a connected app in the Dev Hub and pre-authorize the user
  3. Store the secrets in GitHub (Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions):
    • SF_JWT_KEY – the private key
    • SF_CONSUMER_KEY – the connected app's consumer key
    • SF_USERNAME – the Dev Hub username
    • SF_INSTANCE_URL – the org's login URL

Nothing sensitive lives in the repo; the workflow only reads these secrets at run time.

Step 2: The workflow

Here's the full validate-pr.yml:

name: Validate PR against Scratch Org

on:
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  validate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Checkout code
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Install Salesforce CLI
        run: npm install --global @salesforce/cli

      - name: Authenticate to Dev Hub (JWT)
        run: |
          echo "${{ secrets.SF_JWT_KEY }}" > server.key
          sf org login jwt \
            --client-id ${{ secrets.SF_CONSUMER_KEY }} \
            --jwt-key-file server.key \
            --username ${{ secrets.SF_USERNAME }} \
            --instance-url ${{ secrets.SF_INSTANCE_URL }} \
            --alias DevHub --set-default-dev-hub

      - name: Create scratch org
        env:
          SF_SCRATCH_SIGNUP_CONNECTED_APP: PlatformCLI
          SF_SCRATCH_SIGNUP_CALLBACK_URL: http://localhost:1717/OauthRedirect
        run: |
          sf org create scratch \
            --definition-file config/project-scratch-def.json \
            --alias ci-scratch --duration-days 1 --set-default

      - name: Deploy metadata to scratch org
        run: sf project deploy start --target-org ci-scratch

      - name: Run Apex tests
        run: |
          sf apex run test \
            --target-org ci-scratch \
            --code-coverage --result-format human \
            --wait 20 --test-level RunLocalTests

      - name: Delete scratch org
        if: always()
        run: sf org delete scratch --target-org ci-scratch --no-prompt

A few details worth calling out:

  • --duration-days 1 keeps scratch orgs short-lived, so a failed cleanup doesn't tie up the Dev Hub's active scratch org allocation for long.
  • RunLocalTests runs every test in the org except managed-package tests, which is what a production deployment requires anyway.
  • if: always() on the delete step means the scratch org is cleaned up even when the deploy or tests fail.

The problem that took the longest

Creating the scratch org kept failing even though the JWT login to the Dev Hub worked fine.

The cause: newer Developer Edition orgs use External Client Apps instead of classic connected apps, and the CLI couldn't use my app to sign in to the new scratch org it had just created. The fix was to tell the CLI to use Salesforce's built-in PlatformCLI app for the scratch-org signup step:

env:
  SF_SCRATCH_SIGNUP_CONNECTED_APP: PlatformCLI
  SF_SCRATCH_SIGNUP_CALLBACK_URL: http://localhost:1717/OauthRedirect

After that, the full cycle ran end to end: create → deploy → test → delete.

The result

I opened a pull request with a change, and GitHub Actions validated it automatically against a fresh scratch org. All checks passed, and the PR showed a green tick before merge. Every future change now gets the same treatment, with no manual change sets.

What I learned

  • Git as the source of truth makes Salesforce changes reviewable, just like application code.
  • Scratch orgs are disposable test environments: every run starts clean, so there's no "works in my sandbox" drift.
  • JWT auth plus GitHub secrets is the standard way to give CI access to an org safely.
  • Read the CLI error carefully. The scratch-org failure looked like an auth problem but was really about which app the CLI uses for signup.

What's next

The next part of this project is the release side: protecting the main branch so only validated PRs can merge, and adding Copado to manage environments and promote changes through a pipeline (dev → QA → production). I'll write that up in the next post.

If you're an admin moving into Salesforce DevOps, I'd love to hear how your team handles deployments. Connect with me on LinkedIn.

item.title: Mastering Kubernetes: A Step-by-Step Guide to Pod Troubleshooting
item.description: Kubernetes Pod Troubleshooting Tactics Sequence Kubernetes is a robust container orchestration platform that helps keep applications highly available and…
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
Kubernetes Pod Troubleshooting Tactics Sequence

Kubernetes is a robust container orchestration platform that helps keep applications highly available and scalable. Yet, like any complex system, it can encounter pod-related issues. To tackle these problems effectively, a well-organized troubleshooting approach is essential. In this article, we'll walk through a series of tactics to help you diagnose and fix pod issues efficiently.

Understanding Pods in Kubernetes

In Kubernetes, a pod is the smallest unit you can deploy. It includes one or more containers, along with storage, networking, and configuration settings. When a pod doesn't function properly, it can impact your application's performance or availability. That's why it's crucial to troubleshoot quickly and accurately.

1. Start with Pod Status

Begin your troubleshooting by examining the pod's status.

kubectl get pods

  • Running: The pod is up and running smoothly.

  • Pending: There might not be enough resources available.

  • CrashLoopBackOff: The container keeps failing and restarting.

To find out more details:

kubectl describe pod <pod-name>

2. Examine Pod Events

Events give you a glimpse into what's happening behind the scenes. Check for issues like resource allocation failures, network problems, or configuration errors.

kubectl get events --sort-by='.metadata.creationTimestamp'

3. Analyze Logs

Container logs can often uncover the root cause of a pod's failure. To check the logs, use the following command:

kubectl logs <pod-name>

For pods with multiple containers, make sure to specify the container name:

kubectl logs <pod-name> -c <container-name>

If you find that logs are truncated or missing, make sure that logging is set up properly.

4.Check Resource Utilization

Resource constraints can cause pod failures. Make sure to verify the resource requests and limits:

kubectl describe pod <pod-name>

Keep an eye on usage to make sure pods have enough CPU and memory:

kubectl top pod

5. Inspect Readiness and Liveness Probes

Misconfigured probes can lead Kubernetes to incorrectly mark healthy pods as unready or restart them unnecessarily.
Take a look at the readiness and liveness probe settings in the pod's YAML:

livenessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /healthz
    port: 8080
  initialDelaySeconds: 3
  periodSeconds: 3

6. Validate Configurations

Errors in configurations, like secrets, config maps, or volume mounts, can cause pods to malfunction. Make sure all necessary configurations are correctly referenced:

kubectl get configmap
kubectl get secrets

Review the mounted volumes and ensure their paths are correct.

7. Examine Node Conditions

Occasionally, the problem might be with the node instead of the pod. Take a moment to check the node that is running the problematic pod:

kubectl describe node <node-name>

Check for conditions such as OutOfDisk, MemoryPressure, or NetworkUnavailable.

8.Investigate Networking Issues

Ensure smooth communication between pods and services:

  • Ping another pod using its IP:
  •   kubectl exec -it <pod-name> -- ping <target-ip>

  • Test DNS resolution within the pod:

      kubectl exec -it <pod-name> -- nslookup <service-name>

9. Debug with Interactive Shell

Access the pod’s container to troubleshoot interactively:

kubectl exec -it <pod-name> -- /bin/bash

Inspect configurations, review running processes, or explore file systems directly.

10. Use Diagnostic Tools

Kubernetes provides tools like kubectl debug for advanced troubleshooting. This tool allows you to create a temporary debugging container within your pod, helping you diagnose and resolve issues efficiently.

kubectl debug <pod-name> --image=busybox

Alternatively, you can use tools like Lens or k9s. These tools offer a visual interface that makes troubleshooting easier.

11. Examine Deployment Strategies

At times, the issue might not be with the pod itself but rather with the deployment process.

  • Check rolling updates or other deployment strategies.

  • Go through the deployment YAML to spot any misconfigurations.

12. Engage Kubernetes Logs and Audit Trails

When troubleshooting issues that extend beyond the pod, delve into cluster-level logs or audit trails. These resources can reveal events that might have affected the pod, providing valuable insights for resolving problems.

kubectl logs --previous <pod-name>

Best Practices for Proactive Troubleshooting

  • Use monitoring tools like Prometheus and Grafana to gain real-time insights into your system's performance.

  • Set up logging solutions such as the ELK Stack for thorough log analysis.

  • Utilize Kubernetes-native tools like Kubelet and Metrics Server to keep track of your cluster's health.

Conclusion

Troubleshooting Kubernetes pods might seem challenging, but with a step-by-step approach, it becomes much more manageable. By using these strategies, you can pinpoint the root cause and fix issues effectively, keeping your applications running smoothly and reliably.

item.title: Docker CLI Cheat Sheet: Essential Commands for Containers
item.description: Master Docker CLI commands to manage containers efficiently—a cheat sheet for developers and DevOps engineers
item.dc:creator: Robin Sishodia
item.content:encoded:
In today's software development landscape, Docker is an essential tool for creating, deploying, and running applications smoothly across various environments. The Docker Command-Line Interface (CLI) offers a robust method to work with Docker, manage containers, and efficiently organize your applications. This cheat sheet showcases the key Docker commands that every developer and DevOps engineer should be familiar with.

1. Docker Basics

  • Check Docker Version:
  •   docker --version
  docker version

  • Show System-Wide Information:

      docker info

  • Log in to Docker Hub:

      docker login

  • Explore All Commands and Options:

      docker --help

2.Working with Images

  • Search for an Image on Docker Hub:
  •   docker search <image-name>

  • Pull an Image from Docker Hub:

      docker pull <image-name>

  • List Downloaded Images:

      docker images

  • Remove an Image:

      docker rmi <image-id>

3. Managing Containers

  • Create and Start a Container:

      docker run -it <image-name>

  • Run Container in Detached Mode:

      docker run -d <image-name>

  • List Running Containers:

      docker ps

  • List All Containers (including stopped ones):

      docker ps -a

  • Stop a Running Container:

      docker stop <container-id>

  • Start a Stopped Container:

      docker start <container-id>

  • Remove a Container:

      docker rm <container-id>

4. Accessing Containers

  • Access Container Shell:

      docker exec -it <container-id> /bin/bash

  • Copy Files from Container to Host:

      docker cp <container-id>:<source-path> <destination-path>

  • View Container Logs:

      docker logs <container-id>

5. Managing Docker Volumes

  • List Docker Volumes:

      docker volume ls

  • Create a Volume:

      docker volume create <volume-name>

  • Inspect a Volume:

      docker volume inspect <volume-name>

  • Remove a Volume:

      docker volume rm <volume-name>

6. Docker Networks

  • List Networks:

      docker network ls

  • Create a Network:

      docker network create <network-name>

  • Connect a Container to a Network:

      docker network connect <network-name> <container-id>

  • Disconnect a Container from a Network:

      docker network disconnect <network-name> <container-id>

7. Docker Compose

  • Start Services in Detached Mode:

      docker-compose up -d

  • Stop Services:

      docker-compose down

  • View Service Logs:

      docker-compose logs

8. Docker Cleanup

  • Remove Unused Data:

      docker system prune

  • Remove All Unused Images:

      docker image prune -a

  • Remove All Stopped Containers:

      docker container prune

Conclusion

The Docker CLI is a powerful tool that makes managing containers easier, streamlining workflows and ensuring consistency. Whether you're just starting or you're a seasoned engineer, keeping this cheat sheet nearby will help you manage your containers with confidence. 🚀

Dive into these commands, try them out, and incorporate them into your daily routines to fully leverage Docker's potential!
